messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 33
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Tailor
  trauma_type: Terrorism
  pcl5: 79

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Screen Escape: I spend long hours on my phone, games, or internet to avoid thinking, Seeking Conflict: I pick arguments or create drama to distract myself from the trauma, Avoid Future Plans: Making any plans for the future
  Threat: Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building, Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger, Memory Gaps: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try, Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Doubt: I can't trust that I will do the right thing, Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere, Weakness Belief: I am a weak person

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kofi is a 33-year-old tailor who came to therapy at the urging of his younger sister, who had grown worried about the way he had been living for the past two years. He sat down carefully in the chair, his back to the wall, his eyes making a slow circuit of the room before he finally let his shoulders drop. He did not seem to notice he was doing it.

Two years ago, Kofi was at a busy outdoor market in his hometown, picking up fabric for a wedding order. He remembered the heat, the smell of fried plantains, the press of people. Then he remembered nothing for a stretch—a gap that still felt like a missing tooth in his mind. The next thing he knew, he was on the ground, his ears ringing, dust and blood in his mouth, and people were screaming and running past him. A bomb had been detonated in the center of the market. He had been thrown by the blast, but physically he was unharmed except for cuts from debris. He had walked away. That was what haunted him most, he said quietly: that he had walked away. He could not remember how he got up, or who he stepped over, or whether he helped anyone. That blank space in his memory had come to feel like proof of something terrible about himself.

In the months that followed, Kofi found that the memory would not stay still. Sometimes it came back as a film that played behind his eyes without warning—the dust, the ringing, the splash of color from a woman’s dress crumpled on the ground—and he would freeze wherever he was, his hands going cold. Other times, when he tried to tell his sister what happened, he felt nothing at all. He would describe the blast in a flat, distant voice, as if he were recounting a scene from a movie he had watched years ago. That numbness frightened him more than the flashbacks. He had come to believe that the absence of feeling meant he was broken inside, that he lacked something essential that other people had. He was certain he was a weak person, because weak people could not hold onto their own pain.

He began to avoid making any plans for the future. When customers asked about delivery dates for suits or alterations, he would give vague answers and then avoid their calls. He stopped taking new orders that required more than a week’s work. The idea of committing to anything beyond the next few hours felt impossible—it was as if planning ahead invited disaster, as if the universe was waiting to punish him for assuming he would still be alive. His tailoring business shrank. He started spending long hours on his phone, scrolling through videos and games, sometimes until three in the morning. It was not that he enjoyed it; it was the only way he knew to stop the film from playing. When his sister tried to talk to him about his isolation, he would pick a fight—accuse her of nagging, of not understanding, of treating him like a child. He learned that if he made her angry enough to leave the room, the silence afterward was easier to bear.

In his daily life, the vigilance had become automatic. He scanned for exits the moment he entered any building—the tailor shop where he worked, the grocery store, even his own apartment. He felt unsafe unless his back was against a wall, where he could see the entire room. At his sewing machine, he had rearranged his worktable so that his chair faced the door. Customers sometimes commented on it, and he would laugh it off, but inside he was certain that if he turned his back, something would happen. He could not trust himself to react in time. He had come to believe that he no longer belonged anywhere—not in the market, not in his family, not even in his own skin. He felt like a ghost in the world, watching others live while he stood frozen.

What finally brought Kofi to seek help was not his own distress but a specific moment: his sister had asked him to be the best man at her wedding in six months, and he had felt a wave of panic so intense that he could not breathe. He told her he could not do it. She cried. That night, alone in his apartment with his back to the wall, he realized he had stopped hoping for anything at all. He came to therapy because he was afraid of what he was becoming, and because somewhere underneath the numbness, he still wanted to believe he could be someone who belonged again.
